PullRequest.Title: agentHost: keep the chosen Copilot account when clients re-send the other one
PullRequest.Body:

> **On hold.** This stays a draft until the design for switching between a GitHub and a Microsoft account is settled. The case below is reached today only through the editor window's welcome screen, which shows its sign-in buttons to a user who is already signed in; that is tracked in #349296.

## For humans

**The bug.** You have the Microsoft Copilot setting on and you are signed in to Copilot with GitHub. You click **Continue with Microsoft**. The Microsoft sign-in works, then you get an error, and you are still on GitHub.

**How you get there.** Once you are signed in with GitHub, the Agents window no longer offers a choice of account. But the first-run welcome of an editor window ("Welcome to VS Code") always shows its sign-in buttons, including Microsoft, even when you are already signed in. So: sign in with GitHub in the Agents window, open an editor window for the first time, and click the Microsoft button on its welcome screen.

**Why it happened.** Copilot runs on one account at a time, GitHub or Microsoft. There is no "use this one" switch: whichever sign-in a window sent last wins. And every open window re-sends a sign-in as soon as Copilot says it is missing. So the two fought each other:

1. You click Continue with Microsoft.
2. Copilot drops the GitHub sign-in and announces "GitHub sign-in missing".
3. Every open window answers at once with the GitHub sign-in it still has.
4. Copilot reads that as "the user chose GitHub" and drops Microsoft. Setup fails.

**The fix.** Copilot no longer asks for the sign-in you just replaced. In step 2 it stays quiet, so the windows have nothing to answer and setup completes. If you cancel the Microsoft setup, it asks then, and the windows hand GitHub back.

**What you will see**

| You do this | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Signed in with GitHub, click Continue with Microsoft | Error after the Microsoft sign-in. Still on GitHub. | Setup completes. Copilot answers from Microsoft. |
| On Microsoft, a GitHub sign-in arrives | Switches to GitHub, then straight back to Microsoft | Switches to GitHub and stays there |
| Signed in with GitHub, Microsoft setup fails, press Cancel | GitHub came back by itself before you answered | Back on GitHub in every window, and it stays |
| Sign out of GitHub | Signed out | Signed out (no change) |

**What does not change.** Anything with the setting off. Anyone who only uses GitHub.

**Still not fixed (follow-up work)**

- Open or reload a window while on Microsoft, and that window can switch everything back to GitHub.
- With no GitHub account signed in, cancelling a Microsoft setup does not stick: Microsoft comes back.
- If a Microsoft setup fails, Copilot is signed in to neither account until you press Retry or Cancel.

**Try it.** In a new profile, turn on `chat.agentHost.copilot.m365.enabled`, sign in to Copilot with GitHub in the Agents window, open an editor window, and click the Microsoft button on its welcome screen. Setup should finish and the model list should change to the Microsoft one.

The rest of this description is the detail for reviewers.

## Summary

With `chat.agentHost.copilot.m365.enabled` on and a GitHub account already signed in to Copilot, choosing Continue with Microsoft completed the Microsoft sign-in and then failed, and the windows stayed on GitHub.

The Agent Host offers a GitHub and a Microsoft sign-in side by side and takes a credential that arrives as the choice of its account. When it dropped the GitHub token because the user chose Microsoft, it announced the GitHub credential as expired. Every connected window still held that credential and sent it back within milliseconds, which the host took as a switch back to GitHub. The same happened in the other direction: when a GitHub sign-in replaced Microsoft, the host announced the Microsoft sign-in as expired, the windows supplied it again, and the host went back to Microsoft.

The host now holds back the request for the sign-in that the user's choice replaced:

- The GitHub request is held from the moment the Microsoft sign-in is taken until the host's Microsoft setup settles. After that the account decides: once the account is Microsoft, or its setup has failed and is waiting for Retry or Cancel, the GitHub request stays hidden; when the setup is given up, the request is shown again and the windows return the GitHub credential.
- The request for a revoked Microsoft sign-in is held once a GitHub sign-in is in place. It is also no longer published in the moment before the account leaves Microsoft, where a pending GitHub request comes first.
- A GitHub sign-out or token loss asks for GitHub as before. It does not hand the account back to Microsoft.
- Microsoft requests that the runtime itself raises are published as before.

The rule lives in `selectCopilotAuthenticationRequirement`, a standalone function that `CopilotAgent` uses to compose `authenticationRequired`. What marks a Microsoft sign-in as revoked is stated next to the code that revokes it (`isRevokedEntraSignIn`). No Agent Host Protocol change and no client change. Nothing changes with the setting off, or for a GitHub sign-in with no Microsoft sign-in involved.

The second commit only moves the rule out of `CopilotAgent` and reshapes the tests. It changes no behavior.

## Validation

Windows, on this branch:

- `pnpm run build-fast` - passed.
- `pnpm run typecheck-client` - passed.
- `scripts\test.bat --run <files> --reporter dot --ci` for `copilotAuthenticationRequirement.test.ts`, `copilotEntraAuthentication.test.ts`, `copilotAgent.test.ts`, `copilotAccountService.test.ts` and `copilotSessionLauncher.test.ts` - **1447 passed**.
- `scripts\test.bat --run src\vs\platform\agentHost\test\node\agentSideEffects.test.ts --reporter dot --ci` - **317 passed**.
- `scripts\test-integration.bat --run <files> --reporter spec --ci` for `copilotAccountContext.integrationTest.ts` and `copilotEntraAuthentication.integrationTest.ts` (native account fixtures against the bundled runtime) - **3 passed**.
- `pnpm run oxlint <changed files>`, `node build\hygiene.ts <changed files>`, `pnpm run valid-layers-check` and `git diff --check` - passed.

Tests:

- A table test of the rule covers each combination that matters, including the two that must not be held: a Microsoft request from the runtime while GitHub is signed in, and a GitHub request while a Microsoft request is pending.
- An agent test models a window that answers each request once with a credential it still holds, with a GitHub sign-in: choosing Microsoft, giving that setup up, choosing Microsoft again, a GitHub sign-in while on Microsoft, and a GitHub sign-out.
- A test next to the Microsoft sign-in code checks that only a withdrawn sign-in is recognized as revoked, not what the runtime asks for.

With the rule put back to what it was before this change, the table test and the agent test both fail, the agent test with the host going back and forth between the two accounts.

### Checked live

The live checks were run on the first commit. The second commit changes no behavior and was validated by the tests above only.

In fresh profiles with the setting on, a GitHub account and a Microsoft 365 account, on Copilot SDK 2.0.0 with its bundled runtime 1.0.113. Unless noted, the runtime was pointed at a pre-production Microsoft 365 endpoint with the `COPILOT_LOKI_BASE_URL` environment variable.

- Two windows, GitHub signed in, then Continue with Microsoft: setup completed, and a message with a specific model was answered by Microsoft 365.
- A GitHub credential arriving while on Microsoft (here from a window reload, see below): the host switched to GitHub and stayed there, and a message was answered by GitHub Copilot.
- Signing out of GitHub after that: both windows were signed out and the host was on neither account. Microsoft was not supplied again.
- Two windows, GitHub signed in, Continue with Microsoft with the default Microsoft 365 endpoint so that setup fails: while the Retry/Cancel dialog was open the host was on neither account; after Cancel both windows returned the GitHub credential and the host ended on GitHub. Microsoft was not supplied again.
- A single window, GitHub signed in, then Continue with Microsoft: setup completed and the host listed the Microsoft 365 models. No message was sent in this case.

### Not covered by this change

- A window that opens or reloads while the host is on Microsoft, and whose account is GitHub, sends its GitHub credential when it connects, and the host switches to GitHub. This was observed in the live check. The same applies to a GitHub credential whose value changed. The host cannot tell these from a new GitHub sign-in. This is follow-up work.
- With no GitHub sign-in, giving up a Microsoft setup still does not last: the host asks for the Microsoft sign-in and a window that holds it supplies it again. This is unchanged and is follow-up work.
- By design, the held Microsoft request is not released when GitHub is later signed out or its token is lost: the host cannot tell the two apart, so it asks for GitHub as before. The held request is dropped when Microsoft is chosen again.
- While a failed Microsoft setup waits for Retry or Cancel, the host is on neither account. Before this change the GitHub credential came back by itself at that point, as a side effect of the defect.

### Not checked

- A successful Microsoft setup against the default Microsoft 365 endpoint.
- An account with enterprise GitHub through Microsoft.

RegressionFixes.Mechanism: During Microsoft sign-in from a legacy GitHub account, clearing the GitHub token published an expired GitHub requirement before the account became Microsoft. Connected clients could each re-send their retained GitHub credential, causing the authentication sequencer to revoke Microsoft again, reset its login attempt and request another runtime restart. The reciprocal revoked-Microsoft notification could initiate another account setup. Client recovery coalesces per resource per connection, so this is redundant account-transition work and cross-window fan-out, not evidence of an unlimited loop.
RegressionFixes.Symptom: An account choice could trigger additional runtime teardown/restart, cancellation and deletion of the Microsoft authentication session, and redundant model-catalog refreshes instead of completing one account handoff. Static call-path evidence establishes the extra work; no duration measurement is claimed.
RegressionFixes.FixedBehavior: The new replaced-sign-in marker hides GitHub's requirement before its token is cleared; the selector also hides revoked Microsoft identity requirements when another account replaced them. Clients therefore do not initiate the unnecessary reverse handoff. Runtime-originated service challenges remain eligible, and cancellation can restore the GitHub requirement.
RegressionFixes.Evidence: The deleted base derived fallback at copilotAgent.ts:1321 exposed _authenticationRequired while the account was legacy. The changed completeAuthentication sets _replacedSignIn to 'github' at head line 4205 before _applyGitHubToken(undefined), and selectCopilotAuthenticationRequirement lines 35-39 suppress the replaced requirement. _applyGitHubToken lines 4120-4130 still records the expired requirement and requests the intended restart. agentSideEffects.ts:748-752 forwards any selected requirement to emitAuthRequired; agentHostStateManager.ts:3495 broadcasts it through the root notification path. agentHostChatContribution.ts:267-272 and agentHostAuth.ts:356-445 show per-connection recovery, invalidation and credential forwarding. A returned GitHub credential reaches copilotAgent.ts:4061-4062, revokes Entra, triggers the onDidRevoke restart at 1670-1671 and CopilotAccountService.reset/release (278-315). _stopClient (4999-5040) stops the spawned runtime, and _ensureClient (5320-5334) starts its replacement. The added agent test at 6097-6141 explicitly models one retained-credential response per resource and checks that choosing Microsoft no longer prompts a reverse handoff. Blame identifies the commit introducing the old account-dependent fallback.

Scenarios.Scenario: Choose Microsoft Copilot while GitHub is active, with multiple connected windows.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Credential forwarding must finish the serialized account handoff, any required runtime stop/start, Microsoft discovery and service activation before setup can complete. Model refresh is scheduled separately, but its catalog is needed for model selection.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Broadcast auth/required and forward retained credentials through authenticate; remote connections use the corresponding network transport.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Before: one replaced-GitHub challenge could reach W windows and elicit up to W first retained-credential replies, coalesced within each connection but not globally. After: zero replies triggered by that suppressed challenge. Genuine Microsoft challenges still propagate.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Clearing GitHub while the account was still legacy exposed its expired requirement and initiated recovery in connected clients.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Credential responses queue reverse account handoffs behind the user's handoff; suppression removes this extra queue work.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Stop and start the shared spawned Copilot runtime.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One shared client per host, with startup and stop promises coalesced; additional sequential reverse handoffs could restart it again before the diff. Counts are per account transition, not per window or model.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The intended token-clear restart already occurred, with reverse credential responses able to trigger additional revocation/restart work.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The intended handoff awaits applicable restart work and runtime acquisition. Busy turns can defer restart.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Create the authentication session; begin/advance/confirm login; cancel/disconnect/delete attempts; read the model catalog.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One authentication session per attempt and one begin plus flow-dependent advances; one grouped model-list RPC per effective refresh, not one per model. Before, unintended reverse handoffs could cancel attempts and initiate another setup.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same SDK operations existed, but client responses to replaced-credential notifications could repeat or cancel them.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Login and activation are on setup's critical path; catalog refresh is deferred and coalesced per scheduling task.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Resolve bundled runtime assets and optionally publish a CA certificate bundle during startup.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One realpath lookup and five parallel existence checks per candidate package during an actual startup; candidate count is platform/layout bounded. Certificate publication is content-addressed, avoiding repeated file writes on warm reuse.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Identical startup work, potentially repeated by unintended extra runtime restarts.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Startup awaits asset resolution and applicable certificate setup before spawning the runtime.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Acquire Microsoft identity/service credentials and supply them to runtime login.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One identity and the small fixed set of requested service resources per setup; setup tracks responses by resource and serializes prompts. Runtime-internal request counts are not exposed by this repository code.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same Microsoft acquisition path existed; reverse handoffs could cancel it or provoke another setup.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Required consent/token acquisition can block discovery or activation; runtime credential waits are bounded to 30 seconds.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: W connected windows, S live unscoped chats affected by handoff, M catalog models, and the login flow's small resource set. Boundary work is grouped by host/runtime or authentication attempt, not M.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Copilot's single authentication sequencer serializes account switches. Windows recover independently. One shared startup is in flight; model refresh triggers coalesce until the scheduled task begins. Login advances and consent prompts are sequential; asset checks run in bounded parallel batches.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Per-connection recovery coalesces by resource/scopes/authorization server; explicit challenges invalidate token-forwarding cache entries. Shared runtime startup and model refresh already coalesce. The new selector returns existing requirement objects, retaining strict-reference notification deduplication. Cold and warm Microsoft setup both retain the existing login operations.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: changed suppression, publication, client recovery, reverse authentication and runtime lifecycle are traced through implementation and added tests.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Frequency of multi-window account switching and native runtime/network duration are unmeasured. SDK-internal network fan-out is not inspectable here.
Scenarios.Verdict: No introduced regression. Suppression removes unnecessary credential fan-out and reverse runtime/account lifecycle work; a concrete performance fix was recorded internally.

Scenarios.Scenario: A GitHub credential replaces an active Microsoft account.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The authentication sequencer revokes Microsoft and applies GitHub credentials; runtime teardown and any necessary restart precede subsequent runtime use. SKU discovery is awaited; model refresh runs separately.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Publish the revoked Microsoft identity request and receive credentials from connected windows.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Before: a revoked identity notification could initiate one recovery per connection/resource. After: zero recovery calls from that suppressed notification; existing GitHub requirements can still be delivered.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The selected requirement could expose Microsoft revocation immediately before or after returning to legacy mode.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Removing Microsoft responses prevents a reverse Microsoft setup from joining the authentication queue.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Restart the shared runtime after Entra revocation and any GitHub credential-mode change.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Grouped per shared client transition; pending reasons and stopping/starting promises coalesce. Duplicate same-token GitHub responses do not repeat token-change work.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same intended revocation/restart occurred, and re-supplied Microsoft credentials could start another handoff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Applicable runtime lifecycle work delays later runtime operations; active unscoped turns defer restart.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: GET /copilot_internal/user for SKU, endpoint and telemetry discovery.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One shared discovery GET per token on cold/expired cache; zero on a valid warm entry. SKU and telemetry callers share the pending discovery. Failed discovery can be retried by later callers, unchanged.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same per-token discovery cache and calls applied to every GitHub handoff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: SKU resolution is awaited during GitHub authentication; telemetry lookup starts independently and shares discovery.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Release Microsoft's authentication session and enumerate GitHub models.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One release sequence for the owned attempt; one catalog RPC per effective refresh, independent of model count.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Identical intended release/catalog operations, with additional Microsoft setup possible after automatic credential replay.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Session release is part of runtime shutdown; model refresh is deferred.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Connected windows W, live chats S, and models M; token discovery groups by actual token rather than by window or model.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One Copilot account-switch sequencer. Client recoveries are independent per connection; shared client lifecycle and discovery calls coalesce. No new parallel burst is scheduled.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The replaced-sign-in marker is a single enum per agent. Setting it repeatedly to the same value is deduplicated. CAPI discovery is per-token coalesced with a 30-minute TTL; account revocation does not newly invalidate that cache.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the new marker is set before revocation, and the selector filters only revoked Microsoft identity requirements. Runtime-originated requirements retain their existing path.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: No timing measurements; exact restart count depends on credential mode, idle state and concurrent lifecycle triggers.
Scenarios.Verdict: No introduced regression. The diff removes an unintended reverse handoff without adding expensive calls.

Scenarios.Scenario: Microsoft discovery fails; the user retries or cancels and returns to GitHub.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Discovery failure releases its attempt. Retry awaits another explicit login attempt. Cancellation revokes Microsoft and restores the outstanding GitHub requirement; GitHub replies must traverse the authentication sequencer before it is usable again.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Cancel/disconnect/delete a failed authentication session and create/login a session for an explicit retry.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One cleanup sequence per owned attempt and one new session per retry. The release path clears ownership and shares an in-progress release; the diff adds no attempt collection or duplicate cleanup.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Identical cleanup and retry operations existed, alongside automatic GitHub recovery that could reverse the failed setup before user choice.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Failure cleanup and explicit retry are awaited; the new finally block only clears a scalar observable.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Request the retained GitHub credential after cancellation.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One newly visible GitHub requirement may elicit up to W client replies, with one pending recovery per connection/resource. Duplicate token application does not trigger repeated token-change teardown.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: GitHub could be requested immediately during the original handoff; cancellation already returned the account to legacy mode.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Credential re-supply is required to restore GitHub after explicit cancellation; it is deliberately withheld while Microsoft setup or its error context owns the choice.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Restart/reacquire the shared runtime, including existing asset filesystem probes when an actual start occurs.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Coalesced per shared client lifecycle, not one subprocess per reply; the same bounded package probes run per actual start.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same runtime operations existed; automatic reverse handoffs could add lifecycle churn before cancellation.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Applicable teardown/acquisition delays restored runtime use or the explicit retry.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: W windows and number of explicit retries. Failed attempts do not accumulate in a new container.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Account switching remains serialized globally for Copilot. Client replies can arrive concurrently, but runtime stopping/starting and per-connection recovery coalesce. Retry is user-driven.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Failure retains Microsoft error context but not an indefinitely growing attempt list. The GitHub request remains an existing single observable value. Warm same-token replies use existing CAPI discovery; failures and negative cache behavior are unchanged.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: failure ownership, finally cleanup, selector state and cancellation reset are directly traced.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Whether a failed setup has created a runtime session and the cost of retry/teardown depend on failure stage. No benchmark data.
Scenarios.Verdict: No introduced performance regression. Deferring automatic account restoration until cancellation is an intentional account-selection tradeoff; it does not independently introduce scaling work or an extra expensive await.

Scenarios.Scenario: GitHub-only authentication, token renewal or sign-out, including Microsoft support disabled.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: GitHub token application and required SKU resolution finish before authentication returns. Sign-out requests a missing GitHub credential and applicable runtime stop; model refresh is deferred.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One discovery GET per cold/expired token cache, shared across callers; none for a valid warm result. Later failure retries are unchanged.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Exactly the same token-keyed discovery and awaiting behavior.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: SKU resolution remains awaited; telemetry work is independent but shares the discovery.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Update static-token sessions, enumerate models, and broadcast GitHub token loss.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Existing sequential updates only for S sessions using static tokens; one grouped catalog read per effective refresh. Token loss emits the same GitHub requirement as before.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Static session updates and applicable restart work are awaited; catalog refresh is scheduled off the authentication path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Restart on token loss, credential-mode changes or failed static-session updates.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Shared/coalesced lifecycle operations per token transition, deferred while unscoped chats are busy.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same restart conditions and startup filesystem setup applied.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Authentication frequency, S static-token sessions and M models. Added selection work is constant-sized per observable recomputation.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Existing authentication sequencer and sequential static-token session updates are unchanged. No added subprocess or network work when Microsoft support is off.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: New state is one scalar enum per agent, not per credential/event/session. The derived selector preserves existing requirement references; strict equality prevents identical selected values from notifying consumers. All existing discovery and model coalescing remain intact.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: changed code introduces only bounded observable state and a constant-sized selector object on this path.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: No measured allocation timing, but the added fixed-size work has no collection growth mechanism.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. Extra observable reads/object construction are bounded and do not defeat downstream notification deduplication.

Scenarios.Scenario: Runtime-originated Microsoft identity/service token challenges and subsequent model/chat use.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Discovery or activation waits for required service credentials, up to the existing credential timeout. Ready-account catalog use can restore its shared authentication session after a runtime restart; a newly opened conversation authenticates through the existing login flow.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Publish genuine credential requirements and receive supplied tokens.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Requirements deduplicate by resource/reason/scopes. The resource set is fixed and small; selected requirement publication remains one at a time, with per-connection recovery coalescing.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same runtime challenges were selected and published.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Required tokens gate login progression; the changed predicate does not hide runtime Required identity requests or Expired service requests.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Acquire or refresh requested Microsoft credentials through the authentication provider.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Setup caches one response/promise per requested resource and serializes prompts; warm credentials may avoid acquisition, while explicit expiration can force refresh. Native provider/network request counts are not visible here.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Same per-resource response tracking, token acquisition and prompt ordering.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Consent/token availability gates discovery or activation.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Restore one shared account authentication session, authenticate conversations, and enumerate models.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: getSession serializes and reuses the existing attempt; one restoration login per missing shared session. Existing conversation login runs per opened/resumed conversation, and catalog enumeration is one RPC per effective refresh, not per model.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Identical shared restoration, per-conversation login and grouped catalog reads.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Restoration gates model/chat runtime use; conversation login gates its own operation. None of these calls is newly introduced or moved earlier.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Small distinct resource count, W connected clients, opened/resumed conversation count and M returned catalog models.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Per-connection recovery coalesces; setup prompts serialize; shared account restoration uses its sequencer. Native SDK/network concurrency is unchanged and not directly inspectable.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Positive credentials and rejected-token challenges retain existing lifecycle. Requirements coalesce and resources are cleared on revocation. The selector filters only the synthetic expired discovery identity associated with revocation; no cache is added or invalidated by the new predicate.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: isRevokedEntraSignIn matches only discovery-resource Expired requirements, while runtime identity requests use Required and service requests use other resources. Implementation and added tests corroborate this distinction.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Actual OAuth/native SDK network behavior and latency are outside static repository evidence.
Scenarios.Verdict: No introduced regression. Genuine runtime challenge work and existing per-conversation boundaries are preserved rather than amplified.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the distinct performance-review pass over all seven changed files and every available diff page against the supplied base. Traced authentication selection, multi-window credential recovery, serialized account switching, runtime lifecycle, attempt cleanup, catalog grouping, filesystem startup work and token caches. No high-confidence diff-introduced performance findings. Recorded one evidenced fix of redundant reverse account-transition/runtime work with base-line blame provenance. Static review; native SDK/provider internal request counts and measured timings remain unavailable.

Stats.CostNote: Copilot SDK reports nano-AI units and model billing multipliers; it does not provide a USD conversion.
